item.title: From Working Group to SIG Architecture: spotlight on AI Conformance
item.content:encoded: Frederico Muñoz and Kirti Goyal (FK): Hi Janet, Yuan, and thank you for the opportunity to learn a bit more about AI Conformance. Can you tell us a bit about yourselves and how you got involved in Kubernetes?: I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. I started my journey writing the core workload controllers that standardized how applications are orchestrated on Kubernetes. Today, I lead SIG Apps as a Co-chair & TL, and also lead the AI Conformance program. My current focus is to ensure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI.: I'm a co-founder of TensorScale AI where we build AI infrastructure for world models. Prior to that, I was a Senior Principal Software Engineer at Red Hat, where I led the development of Red Hat AI platform and upstream open source strategy. I became involved in Kubernetes early on by fostering collaborations between the Kubernetes community and projects I was leading, including Kubeflow, Argo, and KServe. I later helped found and lead WG Serving and the AI Conformance program, advancing innovation and strengthening community collaboration around running AI workloads on Kubernetes.FK: AI Conformance started as a CNCF Program, was it then you got involved? I was actually involved from day one since I pitched the original idea. It became obvious then that everyone was starting to run AI on Kubernetes, but vendors were building their infrastructure stacks in different ways. I got worried about ecosystem fragmentation. So I wrote up the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance Proposal, took it to the CNCF leadership to get their buy-in, and started the AI Conformance Program. Once we had the green light, I reached out to my fellow co-chairs Yuan Tang, Rita Zhang, and Mario Fahlandt to get the community rallied around it. Yes. I was a co-chair of WG Serving at that time and some of the initiatives such as the Gateway AI Inference Extension quickly gained traction. There was a strong interest among the community to include inference-related requirements in the Kubernetes AI Conformance program.FK: How would you describe the motivation behind the creation of the AI Conformance Working Group?: The motivation behind creating the Kubernetes AI Conformance Working Group (AI WG) was to address the rapid convergence of AI workloads onto Kubernetes while preventing ecosystem fragmentation.As AI adoption accelerated, organizations began running increasingly complex workloads, including distributed training, large-scale inference, GPU-intensive pipelines, and emerging agentic AI systems across many different Kubernetes platforms. However, vendors were implementing AI infrastructure capabilities differently, especially around GPUs, networking, scheduling, and inference orchestration. That created portability challenges, operational inconsistency, and growing vendor lock-in concerns.The AI WG was formed to bring the community together around:vendor-neutral AI infrastructure standards,interoperable Kubernetes-based AI platforms,consistent operational behavior for AI workloads,and common requirements for scalable AI deployment.FK: WGs are temporary by nature, based on outcomes: would you say the main goals of the WG were achieved?: Yes, the WG achieved its primary initial goals.The WG has succeeded in moving the ecosystem from: fragmented, vendor-specific AI infrastructure approaches to a shared, community-defined baseline for AI workloads on Kubernetes.Some concrete indicators of success include:Launching the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance ProgramDefining formal Kubernetes AI Requirements (KARs)Getting broad participation from major ecosystem playersGrowing certified platforms from 18 to 31 within a few monthsAligning around newer Kubernetes primitives needed for AI workloadsEstablishing a roadmap for automated conformance verificationMost importantly, the WG created consensus that AI workloads are now a first-class Kubernetes use case.FK: AI Conformance was specifically highlighted at the latest KubeCon: is this a reflection of the growing importance of AI throughout the project?: Yes, the prominence of AI Conformance at the latest KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is a strong reflection of how central AI has become to the Kubernetes ecosystem overall.A few years ago, AI workloads on Kubernetes were still viewed as somewhat specialized, mostly tied to ML platforms or GPU-heavy research environments. What’s changed is that AI is now becoming a mainstream infrastructure concern for nearly every large-scale platform operator.That shift naturally elevates AI from an application running on Kubernetes to a core workload category Kubernetes must optimize for.The AI Conformance initiative reflects that evolution. It signals that the community now sees AI infrastructure requirements, things like accelerator scheduling, high-performance networking, workload-aware orchestration, and low-latency inference, as important enough to standardize at the ecosystem level.Its visibility at KubeCon also shows a broader strategic realization: if Kubernetes is going to remain the universal control plane for modern infrastructure, it needs to provide a consistent foundation for AI workloads across clouds, on-prem, and edge environments.So the emphasis on AI Conformance is not just about chasing AI hype; it's about Kubernetes adapting to a major shift in workload patterns and ensuring the ecosystem evolves cohesively rather than fragmenting into vendor-specific AI stacks.From Working Group to SIG Architecture subprojectFK: How would you describe the change from WG to SIG? Is it a reflection of AI as something that requires ongoing architectural governance?: In Kubernetes, Working Groups are meant to be temporary. Our WG had a specific goal to get the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance requirements published and get the certification process off the ground. Once we hit those milestones, we archived the WG and moved AI Conformance to be a permanent subproject under SIG Architecture.Moving to SIG Architecture definitely proves that AI needs ongoing governance. AI isn’t just a passing trend or a one-off workload. It has become a core part of what Kubernetes runs every day. Because SIG Architecture already owns overall Kubernetes Conformance and API design principles, housing the AI Conformance subproject there makes perfect sense. It makes sure our AI Conformance requirements stay aligned with the rest of the Kubernetes ecosystem for the long haul.FK: And with that change, how would you describe the main goals and areas of intervention of the subproject?: Now that we’re a subproject, our main goal is to keep the AI Conformance standards current, vendor-neutral, and standard-setting. We want to make sure Kubernetes captures the latest advancements in AI infrastructure while keeping the ecosystem fair for everyone. When we find gaps where no clear community pattern exists, we help foster and form new standards to solve them.FK: AI Infrastructure is evolving very quickly, while Kubernetes APIs are designed to remain stable for years. Is this something you consider a challenge?: It’s definitely a tricky balance. AI moves very fast, while Kubernetes is designed to be stable and boring. But we actually structured the program around this exact tension.First, we use a tiered graduation model. When new AI infrastructure concepts emerge, we introduce them as recommended SHOULD requirements. That gives the ecosystem room to experiment and agree on best practices without locking Kubernetes into rigid APIs too early. Once those APIs stabilize and with ecosystem adoption, we graduate them to mandatory MUST requirements.Second, we intentionally keep our focus on the infrastructure layer. We test for core capabilities like accelerator support through Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), rather than getting bogged down in specific AI frameworks or model servers. That keeps the base platform stable while letting the AI tooling evolve as fast as it needs to.FK: DRA has evolved, also due to the work of WG Device Management, as an important part of Kubernetes (and especially so for AI workloads), with SIG Architecture having an important role in how it’s integrated in Kubernetes: do you find any parallel in this? Specifically, do you think there will be a heavier focus in the integration with the evolving Kubernetes architecture as part of SIG Architecture?: There is a huge parallel there. Whenever we face a massive, complicated challenge that touches multiple parts of the codebase and involves multiple SIGs, a Working Group is the best place to start. It lets experts from different SIGs get together to figure out the problem, and build consensus.Being part of SIG Architecture means there will be a much heavier focus on how AI capabilities weave into the evolving Kubernetes architecture. Instead of treating AI as an add-on layer, we’re looking at how core Kubernetes primitives, like scheduling and resource allocation, need to adapt at a foundational level to support the next decade of AI workloads.FK: For interested contributors, what’s the best way to get involved with the AI Conformance subproject?: We're always looking for new contributors. The easiest way to get started is by checking out our main repo at kubernetes-sigs/ai-conformance and join our meetings. If you're interested in defining new AI Conformance requirements, you can jump into PR reviews or propose your own using our KAR template. If you want to write code, we always need help expanding our automated Go test suites in the directory.FK: Any final comments you would like to share?: We’ve been blown away by how fast the community has rallied around this. When we first announced the AI Conformance program during the keynote at KubeCon NA 2025, we weren’t sure what the response would be. But by the time we gave our update keynote at KubeCon EU 2026, we had grown from 18 certified platforms to 31 in just a few months.That kind of growth shows just how much the industry wanted a unified, vendor-neutral standard. It gives organizations the confidence that they can run their AI workloads on any certification Kubernetes platform without getting locked into a proprietary stack.If you’re a platform vendor, we’d love to see you get certified. If you’re a developer interested in the intersection of AI and cloud-native infrastructure, come join us in SIG Architecture!FK: Excellent, thank you both for guiding us in this journey on AI and AI Conformance in Kubernetes.

item.title: Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
item.content:encoded: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on.Why workloads need a shared standardCertified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade.The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use.Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.What the working group will deliverThe charter sets out three deliverables:A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version.A method for testing each requirement against a running workload.Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests.The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc.How the work is organizedTwo Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group.SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group.SIG Apps will bring the application perspective.Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well.The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles.The specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing.Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling.When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments.If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it.And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term.You can find us in on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar.

item.title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
item.author: Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team
item.content:encoded: On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra.Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release.Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded.On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this.On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds.Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to.Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use or to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation.Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust.A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin.Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.Lessons Learned and Future ImprovementsThis was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402).Upgrading and Verifying Your DeploymentsIf you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via or or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.You can verify your current toolchain version using and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m <path_to_your_binary>.The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:$ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest $ govulncheck -mode=binary <path_to_your_binary> Securing Go Deployments EverywhereFor us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.

item.title: How to fund Rust contributors
item.author: Jakub Beránek
item.content:encoded: There is always so much to do in the Rust Project! New features to implement, bugs to fix, performance optimizations to make, issues to triage… It takes a lot of work to keep our high bar of quality while also shipping new features and improvements. And the workload keeps increasing with the continuous growth of Rust adoption.As is unfortunately common in open source projects, a large fraction of that work is currently done by volunteers. That causes various issues, such as people burning out or complex features taking many years to ship.Unsurprisingly, one of the best ways to help improve that is to get more people who work on Rust funded! This year, several funding initiatives started ramping up, and we already experience many positive effects. They helped us improve the maintenance status of critical Rust projects and make significant progress on several long-awaited features, such as allocators, the never type, the next trait solver or the Polonius borrow checker. However, only a fraction of people working on Rust are currently funded for their work.We know that there are Rust users, both individuals and companies, who would like to help improve Rust by funding it, but it might not always be obvious to do that. This post thus provides suggestions on how you can support the development of Rust in three ways.If you're unsure which option fits, or would like to discuss funding on behalf of your company, please contact the Funding team.Maintenance is a continuous process required to keep Rust (or any software project for that matter) working. It consists of two main activities. The first is general housekeeping, such as ensuring that Continuous Integration works, dependencies are kept up-to-date and issues, bugs and security incidents are promptly triaged and resolved. The second is performing refactorings and code reviews, which ensures that the codebase will be able to evolve and continuously ship new features, without accruing extensive technical debt.Having quality maintenance is crucial for the long-term health of Rust, yet it is typically very difficult to find funding for it; funders often want to sponsor specific new features, rather than just "keeping the lights on". However, without sufficient maintenance, it becomes much more difficult, and much slower, to ship new features. Improving the maintenance of Rust thus also helps us ship features and improvements faster, though the effects are sometimes only observable over longer periods of time.Funding maintenance is a great choice if you want to let us decide how best to improve Rust. The Rust Funding team continuously looks for Rust teams and projects that require help with their maintenance efforts, and allocates available funds to Rust maintainers who could help improve the situation. Fund specific features and improvementsThere are always many Rust improvements and new features that are in progress. We track some of those initiatives through Rust Project Goals. Each Goal describes a specific improvement to Rust: what it is, who is going to develop and drive it forward and which Rust teams are willing to help reviewing and maintaining it.Some of those Goals are looking for funding. Either to help their owner dedicate time and focus to push the given feature forward, or to fund maintainers who will perform refactorings necessary to unblock that feature and review its implementation. Often funding is required for both. When a Goal is properly funded, the probability that it will achieve its milestones is much higher, which then translates in the given improvement being shipped sooner to Rust users.Funding Project Goals is a great choice if you want to help push forward specific Rust features or Rust toolchain improvements that will benefit you or your company.To fund contributors working on Project Goals, consider taking a look at Goals that need funding and reaching out to their funding contact. If in doubt how to proceed, reach out to the Rust Funding team. Fund individual contributorsThere are hundreds of people in the Rust Project who continuously work on improving Rust. Some of them have personal fundraising profiles (e.g. on GitHub Sponsors), which allows you to support them directly.There might be various reasons for supporting a specific person. Maybe they are maintaining a crate that you love to use, maybe you like reading their blog posts, or maybe you are simply a fan of the work that they do. Whatever the reason, we are sure that they would appreciate your support!Funding individual contributors is a great choice if you want to directly support Rust contributors whose work you appreciate.To fund individual Rust contributors, check out their GitHub profile or personal website to see what options there are for supporting them. You can also examine our list of Rust Project members who can be supported through GitHub Sponsors.We hope that this post is useful to anyone who would potentially like to invest funds into making Rust better. You can also find a shortened version of the "how to fund Rust guide" at the Funding page of the Rust website, or check out a RustConf 2026 talk by Niko Matsakis about how Project Goals and their funding works.If you are a company looking to fund the development of Rust, consider joining the Rust Commercial Network. Joining the network is free, and Rust Foundation membership is not required. It can help you find opportunities for funding improvements in specific areas related to Rust usage (e.g. user interfaces, language interop, supply chain security, etc.) and collaborate on funding Rust development with other companies.There are of course other ways of helping Rust other than donating funds. For example, you can check out Project Goals that are looking for contributors or more generally check our contributor onboarding guide. Companies can also help by giving employees paid time to contribute upstream, or by hiring Rust contributors to do that work. One possible model is the Engineer in Residence role, that was recently established in the Rust Foundation.

item.title: Help set Go's priorities for next year
item.author: Cameron Balahan, on behalf of the Go team
item.content:encoded: Hi Gophers! The 2026 Go Developer Survey is now open. We run this survey every year to understand how you use Go and the challenges you face. Your answers directly shape how we plan and prioritize our work.Last year, 5,379 of you responded, and your top frustration was making sure your code follows best practices and Go idioms (33% of respondents). Since then, we shipped a rewritten in Go 1.26 that automatically modernizes your code, and added more modernizers in Go 1.27. You can read everything we learned in the 2025 results.Take the survey here. It’s open through , takes about 10–20 minutes, and every question is optional. We’ll share the results on this blog in early 2027.Please share the survey with your colleagues, friends, and online communities—the more Go developers we hear from, the better we understand what you need.Thank you for helping shape the future of Go!

item.title: Announcing rustup 1.29.2
item.author: The Rustup Team
item.content:encoded: The rustup team is happy to announce the release of rustup version 1.29.2.Rustup is the recommended tool to install Rust, a programming language that empowers everyone to build reliable and efficient software. What's new in rustup 1.29.2This is a small release which only updates the rustls-webpki and webpki-root-certs dependencies to address the problematic eMudhra intermediate certificates issue described in CVE-2026-111943.Further details are available in the changelog!If you have a previous version of rustup installed, getting the new one is as easy as stopping any programs which may be using rustup (e.g. closing your IDE) and running:Rustup will also automatically update itself at the end of a normal toolchain update:If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website.Rustup releases can come with problems not caused by rustup itself but just due to having a new release.In particular, anti-malware scanners might block rustup or stop it from creating or copying files, especially when installing which contains many small files.Issues like this should be automatically resolved in a few weeks when the anti-malware scanners are updated to be aware of the new rustup release.Thanks again to all the contributors who made this rustup release possible!

Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as:If you don't have it already, you can get from the appropriate page on our website.Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases:Missing symbol : Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing , and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback.The LLVM pass may introduce calls to as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using , as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns.Miscompilation of FFI return values on x86_64: Rust functions returning through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than or . This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI. failed to load on macOS: This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now is built with an entry for the directory containing .If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider using the beta () and nightly () channels locally and in your CI. Please report any bugs you might come across!Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.1. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

item.title: Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
item.content:encoded: You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect.In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?”The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort.This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example.The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them.First, separate admission from Pod schedulingKueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions.Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads?Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods?That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still , move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events.Kueue admission architectureThe Headlamp-first troubleshooting pathThe quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell.Tracing a pending Job through HeadlampStep 1: Open the Workloads viewIn Headlamp, open . Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it.Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it.Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan:priority and priority classa readable current status such as , , or If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource.Step 2: Read status, conditions, and eventsOpen the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML.For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are and . means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation. with a reason such as means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation.An status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here.For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it.Also check the section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted.Stay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together.This matters because a Job with and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload.If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet.In our example, the Workload requests:600 MiB of memory in totalThe next question is where that request entered Kueue.Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueueUse the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue.The LocalQueue page shows:its namespace and connected ClusterQueuestop policy and current statuspending, reserving, and admitted Workload countsKueue conditions and Kubernetes eventsrelated Workloads in the same namespaceThis page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there?If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it.Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usageA ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues.On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with:nominal quota for each ResourceFlavorcurrent reservations and usageborrowing and lending limitspending, reserving, and admitted Workload countsqueueing strategy and stop policypreemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settingsKueue conditions and Kubernetes eventsFor the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended.This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node.Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when neededQuota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes.If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information.These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned?What we learned without leaving HeadlampFor the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation:The Workload is not admitted.Its condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota.The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots.Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue.The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots.Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes.The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation.If the Workload is admitted, switch viewsSuppose the Workload detail page shows , but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views:Open and inspect the Job state and events.Open and filter by the Job name or namespace.Select a Pod and read its section.At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures.This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article:Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp., but Pods are : investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp.A repeatable Headlamp checklistWhen the next Job does not start, use this short path:Open and select the correct namespace.Find the Workload associated with the Job.Check the readable status, , and conditions.Read the condition message and recent events.Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments.Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue.Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy.Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota.If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views.What Headlamp replaces during this investigationThe plugin does not replace or for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation.Is the Workload admitted?Kueue → Workloads → status and conditionskubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace>Which LocalQueue did it enter?Workload → linked LocalQueuekubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yamlWhich ClusterQueue provides quota?LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueuekubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yamlWhich flavor or shared quota matters?ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohortkubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yamlWhat happened after admission?Workloads → Jobs and Pods → eventskubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read.Optional: reproduce the pending scenarioTo reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota.Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp.Current alpha limitationsThe release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path.The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows.Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable.The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp.Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release.These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect.Developed during LFX MentorshipThe plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system.Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release.Try it and share feedbackIf a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.
